To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a hydromechanal model of the human ear with nonlinear feedback on membrane displacement was developed.

the passive response shows high frequency slopes of about 70 dB/oct and a short wavelength corresponding to 1.0 Bark, and that high frequency slopes and Q10 with one feedback loop agree with animal data.

a PVF2 bending type piezoelectric sensor and actuator for a single-channel hydromochemical model of the human ear was developed and that the high-frequency slopes of 60 dB/oct, the shortest wavelength of 17 mm, and the Q10dB of 0.8 with a single feedback loop were obtained.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following three subjects.
a single-channel hydromoehanical model of the inner ear, which can be used as a tool to study the mechanism of hearing and the effect of cochlear implants.
the following points: (1) The hydromechanic model of the cochlear with nonlinear feedback using piezoelectric PVF2 bending type transducers was constructed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present model is a reasonable representation of the passive cochlea and the active feedback is not yet fully understood.
the hydromechanalical model with the nonlinear feedback is in good agreement with animal data.
the model with PVF2 bending actuators and sensors is capable of reproducing the main features of the human cochlear mechanics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hydromechanically based model with nonlinear feedback using the PVF2 transducers is capable of reproducing most of the features of the mammalian cochlea.
the hydromechanics of the mammalian cochlea is well described by a model with nonlinear feedback and longitudinal stiffness of the basilar membrane.
we could reproduce the passive and dynamic responses of the human cochlear partition in the frequency range from 0.5 to 10 kHz with the model.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the hydromechanics of the cochlea can be modeled using a simple mechanical system with nonlinear feedback, and that this model can reproduce the input impedance, phase response, high-frequency slopes, and dynamic compression of the mammalian cochlea.
the model is a good starting point for the development of a more complete model of the human auditory periphery.
the hydromechanics of the cochlea can be modeled by a single channel with nonlinear feedback.
